questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The weather - I knew I was going during the autumn semester and I didn't want to freeze.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Not very - I had issues getting to the university and the taxi driver, while getting me to the campus, dropped me off at the wrong building. It would have been great if someone had been available to pick me up, since the University pressed me to arrive earlier than scheduled, and that is a service they provide to people who show up at the exact time they scheduled.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: A student greeted me once I finally got to the correct dormitory building, and helped make sure that I understood the system and which parts of the buildings I could access.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: A shared dormitory room, myself and one more person. It was fairly small, but each side of the room had a single-sized bed with two large drawers underneath, a chair and a desk with bookshelves above and a set of drawers beneath the desk on the right. The room had a fridge, and a bathroom just for the two of us.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: The dormitory building had two microwaves available, as well as water fountains (both hot and cold, instantly). I was aware that a shared kitchen existed, but it was closed at the time due to COVID. As for meal plans, another dormitory building had a cafeteria in the lowest level, and they had plans available for both breakfast, lunch, dinner, or a combination thereof. Please note that they do not accomodate food allergies.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Become friends with your roomie, or at the very least friendly-ish. You'll be spending a lot of time together, and it can either be the greatest thing ever, or a horror story. Thankfully, mine was the good kind, and I am still good friends with my roomie.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very clean, very cheap, as smack dab in the middle of the entire campus as was physically possible.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The "3" given above does not reflect the experience, but considering that it's been two years since I went on exchange, I frankly don't remember it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I don't recall, sorry!

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The office for international students could provide help if any was needed, whether this just be ordinary things or if you needed help with paperwork.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: 100%, I got all of the classes that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: No clue.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was perfectly balanced, as all things should be. While there was a lot of homework, it balanced out and it was easy to adjust your own level of participation in most classes depending on your energy level that day.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I quite enjoyed it. It was more in the style of lectures, with a little bit of participation, for most of my classes. The language class was very hands-on and reminiscent of UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: "Analyzing K-Movies in the Mass Media" (2 credits), "Introduction to Jeju Mythology" (2 credits), and "Jeju Seen from a World Perspective" (2 credits), as well as the language course.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: "Introduction to Jeju Mythology" - if you have even the slightest interest in folklore or mythology, this class is for you. It was by far my favourite class, and you get to dive into uncommon mythologies where English material is incredibly rare. It if it still the same professor, Hahn, then she is the one who wrote the English material on the subject, and you can ask her about a ton of things.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None, I found myself pleasently surprised that almost everything was included.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The food. As someone with a lot of food allergies, I sustained myself on a diet of pre-boiled eggs from the convinience store, popcorn, instant rice & instant ramyeon. It was not healthy, and I do not recommend this location if you're unable to eat pork/beef. Not being able to eat the local cousine meant that I spent an ungodly amount on "food" every month.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I wish there had been more opportunities to mingle the exchange students and the local students. I love my homies from the exchange class, but we were almost always kept as out own little seperate group and it was hard to make friends.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a sports festival (we were team exchange), as well as a various trips (for the exchange students only) during my semester. We went to a botanical garden, went mandarin picking, walked around an ancient forest, etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Ask you buddy to arrange a hangout between a couple of the exchange students and their buddies as well. A few people's buddies did that (not mine), but from what I heard they managed to then make a friend or two at the local university. But if the university is still offering the mandarin picking trip, it's a must!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hear me out, "Jeju Island Teddy Bear Museum" kind of slaps. On the more physical side, climbing Hallasan should be on everyone's bucket list, as the view from the top is simply stunning (as is both the view up and down the mountain. Lastly, while it can be hard to get to, "Jeju Stone Park" on a foggy day in January is one of the craziest experiences I've ever had - it felt like a place that existed outside of our own world. If ghosts or spirits are real, that's where they live.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was a little hard, actually, though I believe this might be because of the separation that occured between the regular students and the exchange students. Other than that, adapting felt sort of smooth, apart from the jetlag.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Say yes to everything. If the debate club has an event on, go! If your buddy wants you to meet some of their friends, go! If your professor asks if you want to come to an art show along with a few other students, go!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Jeju still feels a bit backwards in regards to LGBTQ+... I didn't tell my buddy until the end of my semester, and good thing that I waited, because she ghosted me afterwards even though I owed her money. Can't win them all, I suppose. Though it would be nice if the host university included "LGBTQ+ friendly" in their buddy applications.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The craftmanship that seemed to be abundant and around every corner. They take great pride in their wares, and in being from Jeju, and it absolutely sold me on the place - I want to go back one day.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Consider if you have food allergies and plan accordingly, make sure to befriend your roomie, and go explore the island every weekend. A small group of us went out to different places or activities once every week, to make sure that we made the most of our time.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring your own bedding. Yes, I'm serious. Go to Ikea, buy a cheap pillow and duvet and leave them in their vaccuum sealed bags, then pack some old covers and linens and bring them with you. It sounds crazy, but when you're going home and don't have space for your bedding, you'll be happy to not have spent an insane amount on it and can pass it on to someone else.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being able to immerse myself in the language and go exploring the island, using what I'd learned in both my language and culture classes.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Food. I'm not kidding when I say I came back home four kilos lighter and in desperate need of food that wouldn't trigger my allergies. Also, keep your meds on you - cross contamination is more likely than you think, and slowly feeling yourself being unable to breathe during language class is not an experience I would recommend.
